procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Election Tribunal refusing to set aside its ex parte order against the appellant in an election petition.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court of Rajasthan challenging the Tribunal's order. The High Court rejected the petition on July 17, 1953, on two grounds: (1) the Tribunal was the authority to decide the sufficiency of reasons for non-appearance, and (2) the appellant's counsel was grossly negligent in not appearing on the hearing date.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court under Article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution of India after the High Court granted a certificate for leave to appeal on December 16, 1953. The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court, quashed the Tribunal's order, and directed the Tribunal to reconsider the matter, taking into account specific factors related to whether the plaintiff was misled and acted with due diligence.

directions: The order of the Tribunal is quashed.
The Tribunal is directed to exercise the discretion vested in it by law along the lines indicated by the Court.
The Tribunal will consider whether the plaintiff was in fact misled or could have been misled if he had acted with due diligence and caution.
The Tribunal will take into consideration the fact that the defendant did enter an appearance and did file a written statement and that issues were framed in his presence.

The Tribunal will consider that the case was fixed for the petitioner's evidence only and not for that of the appellant; and that the petitioner examined all the witnesses he had present and did not give up any of them.

issue.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 226 is confined to determining if an Election Tribunal acted within its jurisdiction, or if it extends to correcting errors of law.

facts: The case involved a decision by an Election Tribunal.
Section 105 of the Representation of the People Act of 1951 stated that every order of an Election Tribunal shall be 'final and conclusive'.

An argument was made that because of this finality clause, the High Court's power of review under Article 226 was limited to only determining whether the Tribunal acted within the scope of its jurisdiction, and not to correct any errors of law it might have made within that jurisdiction.
law: The jurisdiction conferred on the High Courts by Article 226 and the Supreme Court by Article 136 of the Constitution is a constitutional power.
This constitutional power cannot be taken away or limited by a legislative statute, such as Section 105 of the Representation of the People Act.
The High Courts and the Supreme Court are the sole authorities that can finally determine what the 'law of the land' is.
The legality of an act or conclusion exists independently of an inferior tribunal's decision. A tribunal of limited jurisdiction cannot make an illegal act legal simply by its own declaration.
The conclusions of an inferior tribunal are considered 'tentative' and are subject to review by the High Courts and the Supreme Court.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the High Court's jurisdiction was confined to matters of the tribunal's jurisdiction.

The Court held that the power under Article 226 is broad enough to allow High Courts to examine the decisions of tribunals to see if they have 'acted illegally,' which includes correcting errors of law.
The 'finality' clause in Section 105 cannot override the constitutional power of review. Therefore, the jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 226 remains to its 'fullest extent'.
However, the Court clarified that this power is discretionary. High Courts should not act as routine courts of appeal to correct 'mere errors of law.'

This discretionary power should only be exercised when a substantial injustice has occurred or is likely to occur, and petitions should not be 'lightly entertained' in this class of case, bearing in mind the legislative policy for speedy dispute resolution.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 226 is not confined to determining if an Election Tribunal acted within its jurisdiction; it extends to examining the legality of the tribunal's decisions and correcting errors of law. However, this power is discretionary and should only be exercised to remedy a substantial injustice, not to correct every minor legal error.

issue.issue_text: Whether an Election Tribunal has the discretion to permit a party to participate in proceedings from the current stage after an ex parte order has been passed, even if no good cause is shown for the earlier non-appearance.

facts: An appellant in an election petition failed to appear for three consecutive hearings, which led the Election Tribunal to proceed 'ex parte' (in his absence).
The appellant's counsel appeared at the fourth hearing and sought to participate in the proceedings from that point onwards.

The Tribunal refused to allow the counsel to participate, reasoning that because no 'good cause' was shown for the earlier non-appearance, the 'ex parte order' could not be set aside, and therefore the party was barred from the proceedings.
law: The Court distinguished between two separate rights for a party who appears late after an ex parte proceeding has begun.

First, under Order 9, rule 7 of the Civil Procedure Code, a party must show 'good cause' for their absence to have the ex parte order set aside and be 'relegated to the position he would have occupied' had he appeared on time. This essentially rewinds the proceeding.

Second, if no good cause is shown, the party cannot rewind the proceedings but still has a right to appear and participate in the case from the stage at which they join. The court has the judicial discretion to permit this participation on such terms as it thinks fit.
An 'ex parte order' is not a permanent bar; it simply means the court proceeds in a party's absence for a specific hearing. It does not prevent the party from appearing at a future hearing.
application: The Supreme Court found that the Election Tribunal had operated under a 'misapprehension' of the law.
The Tribunal wrongly believed that it had no discretion to allow the appellant to participate unless the ex parte order was formally set aside, which required showing good cause.

The Court clarified that while the Tribunal was correct that no good cause was shown (so the appellant could not, for example, cross-examine witnesses who had already testified), it was incorrect to believe this meant the appellant was barred from all future participation.

The Tribunal failed to exercise its discretion because it mistakenly thought it had none. The appellant had a right to appear through counsel and take part in the proceedings from the stage at which they had then reached.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the Election Tribunal failed to exercise the legal discretion it possessed. The Court accepted that a tribunal has the discretion to permit a party to participate in proceedings from the current stage, even if no good cause is shown for an earlier non-appearance. It directed the Tribunal to reconsider the matter and proceed with the hearing in accordance with this principle.

issue.issue_text: Whether a party against whom an ex parte order is made is barred from appearing and participating in the subsequent stages of the proceedings unless the ex parte order is set aside.

facts: An appellant in an election petition case failed to appear for three hearings.
As a result, the tribunal decided to "proceed ex parte" against him.
When the appellant's counsel appeared at the fourth hearing, the tribunal barred him from participating because the ex parte order had not been formally set aside.
law: The general rule of natural justice is that court proceedings should not be conducted behind a party's back.

Under the Civil Procedure Code (Order IX, rule 6), the court is authorized to "proceed ex parte" if a party fails to appear. This is not a formal, punitive order but a procedural step allowing the court to continue despite a party's absence.
The right to proceed ex parte is a right that accrues "from day to day" at each adjourned hearing where a party is absent, not a single order that mortgages all future proceedings.

Order IX, rule 7 states that if a party appears at a later hearing, they can participate, but unless they show "good cause" for their prior absence, they cannot be relegated to the position they would have been in had they appeared earlier.
application: The Court clarified that there is no such thing as an "ex parte order for non-appearance" that permanently bars a party from future proceedings. The court's decision to "proceed ex parte" is simply a statement of fact that it is continuing in a party's absence on a specific day.

Because the decision to proceed ex parte applies only to the hearing where the party was absent, a party has the right to appear at any subsequent adjourned hearing and participate from that point forward.

However, the party cannot "set back the hands of the clock." They must accept all proceedings that have already occurred in their absence (e.g., evidence already recorded). They join the case at the stage it has reached and cannot undo what has been done unless they successfully apply to have the ex parte proceedings set aside by showing good cause for their non-appearance.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition, holding that a party is not barred from participating in subsequent stages of a proceeding simply because an ex parte hearing was held on a prior date. The party has the right to appear at any later hearing and participate from that stage onwards, though they must accept the proceedings as they find them unless they can show good cause for their earlier absence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 226 is confined to determining if an Election Tribunal acted within its jurisdiction, or if it extends to correcting errors of law.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued that the High Court's jurisdiction under Article 226 is not confined and that it should correct errors of law made by the Tribunal. This is demonstrated by their action of filing a writ petition to challenge the Tribunal's decision on its merits and subsequently appealing the High Court's dismissal of that petition.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, aligning with the High Court's ruling, was that the Tribunal was the sole authority to decide the sufficiency of reasons for non-appearance and that its conclusion on this matter could not be challenged in a writ petition under Article 226.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an Election Tribunal has the discretion to permit a party to participate in proceedings from the current stage after an ex parte order has been passed, even if no good cause is shown for the earlier non-appearance.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that they had a right to appear through counsel and participate in the proceedings from the stage they had reached when their counsel appeared, even if they failed to show good cause for their earlier absence and the ex parte order was not set aside.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, reflected in the Tribunal's order, was that allowing the appellant to 'step in now' would handicap the petitioner (respondent) and be an injustice, especially since the petitioner had closed his case offering minimal evidence under the impression the hearing was ex parte.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a party against whom an ex parte order is made is barred from appearing and participating in the subsequent stages of the proceedings unless the ex parte order is set aside.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that they were not barred from participating in the proceedings from the point their counsel appeared, even though the ex parte order remained in place.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, which the Tribunal adopted, was that a party against whom an ex parte order is passed is barred from appearing or participating until that order is formally set aside.

cases.principle: The jurisdiction under Article 226 is conferred by the Constitution, and limitations cannot be placed on it except by the Constitution itself.

cases.case_name: Durga Shankar Mehta v. Raghuraj Singh
cases.principle: Section 105 of the Representation of the People Act cannot cut down or affect the overriding powers of the Supreme Court under Article 136.

cases.case_name: Raj Krushna Bose v. Binod Kanungo and others
cases.principle: Section 105 of the Representation of the People Act cannot take away or whittle down the powers of the High Court under Article 226.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The jurisdiction of the High Courts under Article 226 and the Supreme Court under Article 136 to examine the legality of decisions made by inferior tribunals cannot be taken away or curtailed by a legislative provision that declares the tribunal's orders to be final and conclusive. The High Courts and the Supreme Court are the final authorities on what is legal, and the legality of a tribunal's act is a part of the law of the land that exists independently of the tribunal's own decision.
obiter: The discretionary powers of the High Courts under Article 226 must be exercised along recognized lines and not arbitrarily.
In exercising their jurisdiction under Article 226, High Courts should not act as courts of appeal or revision to correct mere errors of law that do not cause broad injustice.

It is a sound exercise of discretion for High Courts to consider the legislative policy of speedy dispute resolution, particularly in election cases, and therefore not to entertain petitions for prerogative writs lightly in such cases.
Laws of procedure are based on the principle that, as far as possible, legal proceedings should not be conducted to the detriment of a person in their absence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A party against whom an ex parte order has been passed is not barred from participating in the subsequent stages of the proceedings. While failure to show good cause for the initial absence means the party cannot be relegated to the position they would have occupied had they appeared on time (e.g., they cannot file a written statement as of right), they have a right to appear and participate from the stage the proceedings have reached. The court or tribunal has the discretion to permit such participation, subject to terms and conditions, and it is an error of law to believe it has no such discretion because the ex parte order has not been formally set aside.
legal_tests_applied: Good Cause Test: To be relegated to the position one would have occupied if they had appeared initially, a party must show 'good cause' for their absence. If good cause is not shown, the party cannot undo the proceedings that occurred in their absence but is not barred from future participation.

Judicial Discretion for Ends of Justice: In deciding whether to allow a party to participate after an ex parte order, the court must exercise its discretion by carefully weighing all relevant factors to serve the 'ends of justice'. This includes considering justice not only for the parties but also for witnesses and others who may be inconvenienced, and avoiding 'snap decisions' to afford parties a real opportunity to contest their cases.
why_appellant_lost: The Court agreed with the Tribunal and the High Court that the appellant failed to show good cause for their initial non-appearance, stating, 'We agree with the Tribunal, and with the High Court, that no good cause was shown and so the defendant had no right to be relegated to the position that he would have occupied if he had appeared on 17-3-J 953'.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued the factual point that there was no good cause for the appellant's absence, a finding the Supreme Court upheld. The Tribunal had 'failed to satisfy ourselves that there was any just or unavoidable reason preventing the appearance of respondent No. l himself or of any of his three learned advocates between the I 7th and the I 9th of March. 1953'.
policy_considerations: The laws of procedure are based on the principle of natural justice that, as far as possible, no proceeding in a court of law should be conducted to the detriment of a person in their absence.
The court's endeavor should be to avoid snap decisions and to afford the parties a real opportunity of fighting out their cases fairly and squarely.

The concept of 'ends of justice' is broad and includes not only justice to the parties but also to witnesses and others who may be inconvenienced. The convenience of witnesses, who are compelled to discharge public duties, deserves the greatest consideration.

While High Courts under Article 226 can correct errors of law, their powers are discretionary and should not be used as a court of appeal to correct mere errors that do not occasion broad injustice. This is especially true in election cases, where the legislative policy is for disputes to be decided as speedily as possible.
